The town of Bellwether had a peculiar problem: every clock had begun telling a different time. At the bakery, the copper clock claimed it was noon, though the bread was still frozen. At the station, the pocket watches insisted it was midnight, and the conductor waved them aboard. Meanwhile, the church tower’s silver face had stopped entirely.

I found the clocks gathered in the attic above the clockmaker’s shop, where they sat in mismatched chairs. The smallest was a silver thimble, the largest resembled a melon.

“Why can’t you agree?” I asked.

A red alarm clock replied, “Each of us is correct. Time depends on where you are standing.”

This sounded profound until I noticed everyone had rolled beneath the sloping roof, which made their conclusions rather less impressive.

The clockmaker, a woman named Mara, explained that the town’s clocks were not broken. They were homesick. Generations earlier, each had been made for a different household, place, and purpose. Removed from familiar walls, they had forgotten how to share a morning.

So we returned them where they belonged. The thimble went to a child’s bedside. The melon clock returned to the greenhouse. The wooden one, repaired at last, resumed its duties in the schoolhouse. By evening, nearly every clock in Bellwether struck seven together.

Only the mayor’s office remained dark. When I asked why, Mara smiled and said the mayor had finally discovered the usefulness of a clock that did not tell time.

Instead, it pointed toward whatever mattered most.
